walkthroughs.body_html:
Some things heat up easily. Others don't. 🔥

Specific heat capacity (symbol c) is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.

Bigger c → the material is harder to heat up (and slower to cool down).

The units of c are J/kg°C — joules per kilogram per degree Celsius.

For water, c ≈ 4200 J/kg°C. That means heating 1 kg of water by just 1 °C costs 4200 joules!

Most metals have c around 400–900 J/kg°C — much smaller, so they warm fast.

Water's huge SHC is why radiators, hot water bottles and the ocean are great at storing heat.

It's also why coastal towns have milder weather — the sea soaks up and releases heat slowly.

Metals heat fast (good for pans) but lose heat fast too (bad for storing it).

mcqs.q: Why does a metal spoon in hot water heat up faster than a wooden one?
options: Metal heats up faster because it has a lower specific heat capacity, requiring less energy per degree.
Heat is measured in degrees Celsius and temperature in Joules.
Metals have higher thermal conductivity, so heat is transferred more rapidly through them.
Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.

mcqs.q: What does specific latent heat measure?
options: The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 degree.
Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.
The temperature at which a substance melts or boils.
The energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between heat and temperature?
options: Heat is the energy transferred due to temperature difference; temperature measures average kinetic energy of particles.
Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.
Heat and temperature are the same thing — both measure how hot something is.
Heat is measured in degrees Celsius and temperature in Joules.
